nameStory: The orange hobnail canker gets its colorful name from its distinctive appearance on tree bark. The fungus creates raised, bumpy growths that look remarkably like old-fashioned hobnail boots - those sturdy work boots with metal studs hammered into the soles. The orange part comes from the bright rusty-orange color of the fungal structures that peek through the bark.
description: Orange hobnail canker is a parasitic fungus that attacks hardwood trees, creating distinctive raised bumps and cankers on bark. This plant pathogen belongs to a group of fungi that cause serious diseases in trees by growing inside the bark and wood tissues. The fungus produces small, orange-colored fruiting bodies that emerge from cracks in the bark, giving infected areas a bumpy, studded appearance. Individual cankers can range from small coin-sized spots to large patches several inches across.

idTips.label: Orange fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for bright orange to rust-colored, small rounded bumps pushing through bark cracks - they feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Raised bark cankers
idTips.description: The bark around infected areas becomes swollen and cracked, feeling rough and bumpy compared to smooth healthy bark nearby

idTips.label: Hardwood host trees
idTips.description: Found exclusively on deciduous trees like oaks, maples, and hickories - never on pines or other conifers

idTips.label: Bark texture changes
idTips.description: Infected bark often feels softer and more crumbly than healthy bark, sometimes with a slightly musty smell

idTips.label: Clustered pattern
idTips.description: The orange bumps typically appear in groups or lines following bark cracks rather than scattered randomly

habitat: Orange hobnail canker is found in mixed hardwood forests throughout New England, particularly favoring oak-dominated woodlands and maple-rich areas. It thrives in both lowland and mid-elevation forests, commonly appearing along forest edges where trees may be stressed by changing light conditions. You're most likely to spot it on mature trees that have experienced some form of stress or injury.

seasonality.spring: Orange fruiting bodies become more prominent as moisture increases, making this an excellent time to spot the diagnostic orange bumps emerging from bark cracks.
seasonality.summer: The fungus is most active during warm, humid weather, with fruiting bodies at their most vibrant orange color and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Fruiting bodies remain visible but may begin to fade slightly in color, though the raised bark cankers are still readily apparent for identification.
seasonality.winter: While growth slows, the characteristic bark swelling and any remaining orange structures can still be observed on bare trees, making winter good for canker identification.

funFact: This fungus is like a tree's version of a slow-motion zombie infection - it can keep its host tree alive for years while gradually consuming it from the inside out, turning the tree into a living fungus factory that produces thousands of spores.
confusionNotes: Orange hobnail canker is most commonly confused with other bark diseases or insect damage, but the distinctive bright orange fruiting bodies are the giveaway - no other common tree disease produces such vividly colored bumps. Remember: orange bumps mean hobnail canker, while other cankers tend to be brown, black, or bark-colored.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its alarming name, this canker fungus is actually part of the natural forest ecosystem and rarely kills healthy trees outright. The word 'canker' comes from an old Latin word meaning 'crab,' referring to how the disease seems to 'crab' or spread sideways along the bark.
compareHints: Since orange hobnail canker is the only Endothia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other canker-causing fungi in the same family. Unlike chestnut blight (caused by a related fungus), orange hobnail canker produces distinctly orange rather than yellowish fruiting bodies and creates more localized swellings rather than girdling the entire trunk. The hobnail pattern of raised bumps is also much more pronounced than the flatter cankers caused by most other fungal pathogens.
